title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents
event_hint: arXiv:2608.03392v1 surveys self-evolving coding-agent taxonomies, evidence, timing, and evaluation risks
problem: Conventional coding agents remain largely static while repositories, dependencies, tests, and project conventions change. Agents may repeat mistakes because they do not retain or transform executable feedback and coding trajectories into reusable behavior, memory, skills, tools, or workflow changes.
mechanism: This survey defines self-evolving coding agents as feedback-driven systems that change future behavior or internal components from software-engineering interactions. It organizes the literature by the object that evolves—agent framework, memory, skills/tools, model, or workflow/topology—and adds orthogonal axes for when evolution occurs (task-time, post-task, stage-wise) and what evidence drives it (outcomes, environmental feedback, trajectories). Software-specific signals include tests, compiler errors, runtime traces, lint/CI results, repository history, patches, and code review feedback.

evidence.claim: The proposed object-centered taxonomy covers evolving agent frameworks, memory, skills and tools, models, and workflow or topology structures.
evidence.condition: Survey classification of representative self-evolving coding-agent work.

evidence.claim: The survey separates evolution timing into task-time, post-task, and stage-wise patterns and evidence into outcome, environmental-feedback, and trajectory-derived signals.
evidence.condition: Orthogonal dimensions used to compare heterogeneous systems.

evidence.claim: Repository-level context and executable feedback are distinctive because coding agents interact with tests, compilers, shells, dependency managers, CI systems, and human reviews, but those signals can be incomplete, noisy, or misleading.
evidence.condition: Conceptual synthesis across the surveyed literature; no new benchmark measurement is reported.

evidence.claim: The survey identifies correctness, maintainability, robustness, cost, safety, benchmark overfitting, feedback reliability, stale memory, and generalization beyond the evolved setting as open evaluation challenges.
evidence.condition: Survey discussion of evaluation and deployment risks for self-evolving systems.
evidence.source_locator: PDF pp.15-17, Evaluation and Open Challenges

evaluation_context: This is a conceptual survey, not a new controlled performance experiment. It reviews coding-agent systems that inspect repositories, invoke tools, execute tests, debug failures, and evolve memory, skills, tools, models, frameworks, or collaboration structures. It argues that evaluation should go beyond one-shot pass/resolve rates to include functional correctness, code quality, safety, efficiency, maintainability, robustness, cost, and transfer to held-out repositories, benchmarks, models, or languages.
limitations: The paper is a guiding synthesis of an emerging area rather than a quantitative meta-analysis; it reports no new common dataset, aggregate effect size, latency, token, or success-rate measurement. Taxonomy categories cover heterogeneous prior systems with different definitions and evaluation protocols. The survey notes risks of benchmark leakage/overfitting, noisy or misleading executable feedback, stale or repository-specific memory, increased coordination cost, and weak evidence for long-term maintainability or cross-domain generalization.
project_relevance: The taxonomy gives a useful design checklist for this project: separate evolving memory/context, procedural skills, tool interfaces, and workflow policy, and record the evidence that triggered each change. It supports measuring not only final task success but also Read/Grep/tool-call overhead, feedback provenance, stale-memory failures, cost, and transfer across repositories; it does not itself prove any acceleration mechanism.
